Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette:
Ama was twenty years old and worked behind the counter of a chain pharmacy in a midwestern suburb, counting pills and checking interactions, but her mind lived elsewhere—in a flooded basement in the country she had fled two years earlier. There, during the political unrest that tore through her town, she had been taken by armed men who accused her family of harboring rebels. For three days they kept her in a room that filled with water whenever it rained. They forced her head under the murky surface until her lungs burned, then pulled her up to scream questions she could not answer. She remembered the weight of a boot on the back of her neck, the metallic taste of silt, the sight of another prisoner being dragged away—a woman whose name she never learned. Ama survived because she was young and because the men grew bored, but the woman did not. That guilt sat inside her like a stone.

In the months after her escape and resettlement, Ama began to notice that certain things could pull her back into that basement without warning. The sight of a full sink at work, or a customer’s glass of water, would make her breath catch. Arguments with her boyfriend over small things—whose turn to cook, why she was late—would trigger a cold panic, because being forced into a corner felt identical to being forced underwater. And that panic brought with it a quiet certainty: she was being punished for having survived, and the argument was proof she did not deserve peace. And when a manager pressured her to stay late, she felt the same helplessness, the same rage. Each time one of these triggers appeared, she found herself slipping into fragments of memory: her body would tense into the exact arched position she had held when the water covered her face, even as she stood dry and safe behind the pharmacy counter. She could never remember the whole sequence—only flashes of cold, pressure, and the sound of shouting. She could not put the event into words; when her boyfriend asked what had happened to her, she would shake her head and say nothing, because the story had no language.

Ama had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, that if she relaxed for a single moment something terrible would catch her unaware. On the nights when that sense of danger pressed hardest, the full memory of the basement would break through, as if her body were replaying the event to remind her why the vigilance was necessary. This hypervigilance meant that she scanned every customer who entered the pharmacy, noting exits and blind spots. She avoided the break room because it had no second door. When she tried to sleep at night, she lay rigid, listening for footsteps on the stairs, her body refusing to surrender to unconsciousness because being asleep felt too much like being underwater. She told herself she deserved this suffering—that she had survived when the other woman did not, so she had no right to rest. Every time that thought surfaced, the memory of the woman being dragged away came with it—clearer, more intrusive—as if her guilt were pulling the image out of the past to punish her. This punishment thinking kept her trapped in a loop: the more she believed she should suffer, the more she watched for danger, and the more she watched for danger, the more she noticed triggers. A bag of ice melting on the counter would become a flood. A raised voice from a customer would become an interrogation.

She had developed a set of habits to manage the terror. She avoided the hour before dawn because that was when the nightmares came most vividly, and she was certain that if she let one of those dreams take hold, she would not be able to recover. She avoided coworkers who had dark skin and a particular build—men who reminded her of the guards—and she knew this was irrational, but she could not help it. Whenever a memory surfaced, she pushed it away immediately, telling herself that if she started to think about the event, she would fall apart completely and never pull herself back together. But the effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close—she had thought about not thinking about it every day for two years, and the memory had never had a chance to fade. But pushing the memory away only confirmed its power—she never let her mind finish it, so the threat it carried stayed raw, unprocessed, and as immediate as the day it happened. This thought avoidance meant that the memories stayed fragmented, nonverbal, locked in her body but unreachable by words. The incomplete picture haunted her more than the flood itself: she could feel the water in her lungs but could not remember how she got out.

The cycles had tightened over the past year. Her boyfriend had started to pull away, confused by her abrupt silences and her refusal to go to the lake or even to the pool at the gym. At work, she had begun mapping escape routes in every room, scanning the parking lot for cars that looked out of place, and her concentration suffered. A customer complained that she seemed distracted. Her manager suggested she take a leave of absence. That was what finally brought her to a clinic: the fear that she was losing the one thing she had built after escaping. But what frightened her most was the thought that, if she stopped being vigilant for even a moment, the water would find her again. She hoped—barely—that talking to someone might help her find the words she had lost.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt, deserving suffering) directly cause or lead to trauma memories.
The vignette does not convey that a sense of threat causes or elicits trauma memories.
The vignette does not indicate that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance) cause or increase a sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt, deserving suffering) directly cause or lead to trauma memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not convey that a sense of threat causes or elicits trauma memories.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not indicate that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance) cause or increase a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
